item.content:encoded:
From the infectious rhythms of Latin music to the unmistakable pulse of Afrobeats, Desperados and Young Jonn are bringing two cultures together on “Let It Go,” a new track inspired by living in the moment.

Some moments are best enjoyed without overthinking them: a spontaneous night out, an unexpected link-up with friends, or the song that gets everyone moving. Capturing this spirit of freedom and self-expression, Desperados has teamed up with award-winning Afrobeats producer, songwriter and artist Young Jonn for “Let It Go.”

Produced by Yung Willis, the Grammy-nominated music producer whose production credits span some of the biggest names in African music. Having worked with notable artistes including Falz, Wizkid, Kizz Daniel, Davido, Niniola, BNXN, Zlatan, Patoranking and Ice Prince, Yung Willis brings his production expertise to the collaboration, helping shape a sound that connects global influences with the energy of Afrobeats.

Rooted in the brand’s identity and association with self-expression, Desperados continues to find meaningful ways to connect with the younger audience through music, culture and premium experiences. With “Let It Go”, the brand is using music as a touchpoint between its Latin roots and the energy of Nigerian culture.

At the heart of the collaboration is “Guao Guao,” the reggaeton track Desperados created in partnership with Venezuelan artist Micro TDH and Colombian producer Ovy On The Drums. Built around a sample of this unique record, Let It Go brings a Latin-inspired sound into Young Jonn’s style, creating an Afrobeats song that reflects Nigeria’s vibrant music and nightlife culture.


“Let It Go” is more than a fusion of two sounds. It is an expression of the Desperados vibe, where music becomes a way to encourage people to loosen up and enjoy moments that make life memorable. By connecting the global influence of Latin music with Afrobeats, the brand reinforces its place through music, culture, and self-expression.

Young Jonn’s ability to reinterpret global influences through a distinctive Nigerian style makes him a fitting partner for this expression. Rather than recreating the original, he gave the sound a fresh identity, shaped by the rhythm and movement of Nigerian music. Whether it’s the rhythm that takes over the dance floor, an ordinary link-up that turns into a memorable experience, the song captures the freedom of letting go and being fully in the moment.


For Desperados, the brand’s involvement gives the song a cultural expression, connecting its identity to a sound that brings people together, encourages movement and creates room for memories. From recreating dance moves to sharing interpretations through lifestyle content, fans can join the “Let It Go” vibe beyond simply listening.

item.content:encoded:
Ecclesia Hills Church is pleased to announce the sixth edition of the Ecclesia Word Conference, themed “Freedom in Christ.” The conference will take place from Friday, 6th November to Sunday, 8th November 2026, at The Hall, 16 Musa Yar’adua Street, Victoria Island.

The Ecclesia Word Conference has grown into a gathering where believers are taught, equipped, and stirred to live out the fullness of their faith. Last year’s edition explored the theme Custodian of Holy Oracles. This year’s edition turns to a question at the heart of the Gospel: What is freedom in Christ, and how can the Ecclesia arrive there?

“This conference is crucial to bringing believers to the accuracy of freedom,” said Pastor Moses Ida-Michaels, Pastor of Ecclesia Hills Church. “Many people carry the name of Christ yet remain bound by religion, fear, habits, financial pressure, and generational patterns. This gathering is about seeing freedom clearly and walking in it. Together, we will hack the principles that bring true liberty to life,” he concluded.

Across three days, sessions will address freedom in every area of life, including:

  • Free a Generation: El-Shakar

item.title: More Than Just a Glass of Milk: A Dietitian’s Perspective on Why Milk Matters
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Written By Tito Ipinmoye

The post More Than Just a Glass of Milk: A Dietitian’s Perspective on Why Milk Matters appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
If you grew up in Nigeria in the 90s or early 2000s, chances are you didn’t learn about milk from a science class. You learnt about it from television.

Back then, adverts were part of our childhood. We didn’t reach for a remote every time the commercials came on. We sang the jingles, quoted the catchphrases and years later, many of us can still remember them word for word.

For me, one advert stands above the rest. It followed a young Kanu Nwankwo as he dribbled a football through the dusty streets of Owerri on an errand for his mother.

He left home with nothing but a football at his feet, dribbling all the way to the market. Just as a tin of milk slipped from the market woman’s hands, he flicked it back into the air with effortless skill.

She smiled and said, “Papilo, I know say one day you go make us proud.”

As children, we believed her.

Not because we understood marketing, but because those adverts made us believe that greatness could begin anywhere. They told us that a boy from Owerri, Nigeria could become one of Africa’s greatest footballers. They told us that ordinary children with big dreams could grow into extraordinary adults.

And somewhere between that advert and my mum pouring Milk into my breakfast cereal every morning before school, I came to believe two things.

The first was that milk helped build strong bones and teeth. The second was that maybe, just maybe, I could become whoever I dreamed of becoming.

Years later, after becoming a dietitian, I realised that my childhood understanding wasn’t wrong, it was simply incomplete.

Today, conversations about milk have become surprisingly complicated. Social media is filled with conflicting opinions. Some people insist milk is only for children. Others believe it causes weight gain. Some assume all milk is the same, while others believe dairy milk and non- dairy offer identical nutrition.

As nutrition professionals, we know that the truth is rarely found in headlines or viral videos. It is found in evidence.

So, let’s separate what we know about milk from what we only think we know.

What Exactly Is Milk?

From a scientific perspective, milk is the natural nutrient-rich fluid produced by mammals to nourish their young during the earliest stages of life. For humans, cow’s milk is the most widely consumed form of dairy milk and has been part of diets around the world for generations.

But from a nutrition perspective, milk is much more than its definition.

It is a naturally nutrient-dense food that provides a unique combination of high-quality protein, calcium, phosphorus, vitamin B12, riboflavin and other essential nutrients that work together to support growth, bone health, muscle function, energy production and overall wellbeing throughout life.

Unlike many foods that contribute just one or two key nutrients, milk delivers several essential nutrients in one convenient food. This is one of the reasons it has remained a staple in many cultures and continues to play an important role in healthy eating patterns across different stages of life.

Yet despite these nutritional benefits, milk remains one of the most misunderstood foods on our tables.

Over the years, I’ve heard people say that milk is only for children, that it causes weight gain or that all milk products are the same. Social media has only amplified these conversations, making it increasingly difficult to separate evidence from opinion.

So, let’s look at some of the most common myths about milk and what science tells us.

Why Milk Matters

One of the things I have learned after years of working as a dietitian is that conversations about milk often focus on just one nutrient: calcium.

Yes, milk is well known for supporting strong bones and healthy teeth, but that’s only one part of the story.

Milk provides a unique combination of nutrients that work together to support the body in different ways. Rather than contributing just one benefit, it supplies several essential nutrients in a single food, each playing its own role in maintaining good health.

High-quality protein helps build and repair muscles, organs and other body tissues. It’s essential for growth in children and helps adults maintain muscle mass throughout life.

Calcium and phosphorus work together to support strong bones and healthy teeth. These nutrients are especially important during childhood and adolescence, when bones are developing rapidly, but they also remain important throughout adulthood to help maintain bone health.

Vitamin B12 plays an essential role in the production of healthy red blood cells and supports the normal functioning of the nervous system. Riboflavin (vitamin B2) helps the body convert the food we eat into the energy we need for everyday activities.

Many Milk products are also fortified with vitamins A and D. Vitamin A supports healthy vision and the normal functioning of the immune system, while vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium effectively, making it an important partner in maintaining strong bones.

What makes milk unique isn’t that it contains one remarkable nutrient. It’s that it brings many important nutrients together in one food.

That combination is one of the reasons milk has remained part of healthy dietary patterns across different cultures and generations.

A glass of Milk doesn’t provide just one nutrient.

It provides a package of nutrients working together to support growth, development and overall wellbeing.

Myth 1: “Milk Is Only for Children”

One of the most common misconceptions I hear is that milk is something we eventually outgrow, that once we become adults, it no longer has a place in our diet. I understand where that idea comes from.

Many of us first encountered milk as children. It was stirred into our morning pap, added to cereal before school or mixed into a warm cup of tea on rainy days. Over time, it’s easy to begin thinking of milk as a “children’s food.” But our bodies tell a different story.

While our nutritional needs change throughout life, they never stop. In fact, the nutrients milk provides continue to support us in different ways as we grow older.

For children, milk contributes high-quality protein, calcium and other essential nutrients that support healthy growth and the development of strong bones and teeth. During the teenage years, when growth accelerates and nutritional demands increase, these nutrients remain just as important.

As adults, the focus shifts. Growth may slow, but maintaining muscle mass, preserving bone health and meeting our daily nutrient needs become priorities. The high-quality protein, calcium and other vitamins and minerals found in milk continue to contribute to those goals as part of a balanced diet.

For older adults, maintaining muscle strength and bone health becomes increasingly important. Adequate protein helps preserve muscle as we age, while calcium and vitamin D, where milk is fortified with vitamin D, continue to support healthy bones.

In other words, milk doesn’t stop being relevant because we grow older, its role simply changes. The nutrients remain valuable. What changes is how our bodies use them at different stages of life. Perhaps that’s a better way to think about it.

Milk grows with us, not because every person must drink milk every day, but because the nutrients it provides continue to support health from childhood through older adulthood as part of a healthy, balanced diet.

Myth 2: “Milk Causes Weight Gain”

If you’ve spent any time on social media, you’ve probably come across someone confidently declaring that milk is “too fattening” or should be avoided if you’re trying to manage your weight. It’s a message that’s repeated so often that many people now accept it as fact. The reality, however, is much less dramatic.

No single food causes weight gain on its own. Weight gain occurs when, over time, we consistently consume more energy than our bodies use. Overall dietary patterns, portion sizes, physical activity, sleep and other lifestyle factors all play a role.

This is why it’s important to understand the different dairy milk options available rather than assuming they all have the same nutritional profile.

Full Cream Milk naturally contains milk fat and provides high-quality protein, calcium and a range of essential vitamins and minerals. It can be enjoyed as part of a healthy, balanced diet by individuals and families whose nutritional needs and preferences align with this type of dairy milk.

Filled Milk, on the other hand, is a dairy milk product in which part or all of the natural milk fat has been replaced with vegetable oils. While its fat composition differs from that of Full Cream Milk, it continues to provide important nutrients such as protein and calcium, giving consumers another dairy milk option to suit different nutritional needs and preferences.

The important question, therefore, isn’t whether milk is “good” or “bad.” It’s whether the product you choose fits your overall dietary pattern, lifestyle and nutritional needs. Nutrition is rarely about eliminating one food, it is about building balanced eating habits over time.

Myth 3: “All Milk Is the Same”

At first glance, it’s easy to see why many people believe all milk is the same. Walk into any supermarket and you’ll find shelves lined with products that look similar, often displayed side by side. But while they may all be found in the same aisle, they are not all the same.

One of the biggest misconceptions I encounter is the belief that every white powder added to tea, coffee or cereal is simply “milk.” These products are designed for different purposes, and understanding those differences is an important part of making informed nutrition decisions.

Broadly speaking, consumers will come across three main categories:

● Dairy milk, such as Full Cream Milk and Filled Milk, which provide high-quality protein, calcium and other essential nutrients.

● Creamers, which are designed primarily to add creaminess, texture and flavour to beverages such as tea and coffee. They serve a different purpose from dairy milk and do not provide the same nutritional profile.

Ultimately, the best choice begins with understanding what each product is intended to do. When we know the difference between dairy milk, and creamers, we can choose the product that best fits our nutritional needs instead of assuming they are all nutritionally equivalent.

Final Thoughts

Whenever I think about milk, I don’t think first about football. I think about the words of a mother to a young boy: “Papilo, I know say one day you go make us proud.”

As children, we saw a story about dreams. Looking back, I realize that the advert gave us more than nostalgia. It sparked a conversation about nutrition that many of us are still having today.

The difference is that, as adults and for me, as a dietitian we now have the opportunity to replace assumptions with evidence. We can look beyond the stories we grew up with and make informed choices based on nutrition science.

The stories that shaped our childhood sparked our curiosity. Science helps us make informed choices. And that’s something worth passing on to the next generation.

item.content:encoded:
On Monday, 12 October 2026, adidas and waf. (Wflsncrm) release the Superstar ADV worldwide, marking the first time an African skate community has shaped the silhouette since its 1970 debut.

Co-established in 2012 by Jomi Marcus-Bello, Nifemi Marcus-Bello, and KC Obijiaku, waf. has spent 14 years nurturing the Lagos skateboarding scene from the ground up, culminating in the opening of a skatepark at Freedom Park, located on the site of a former colonial prison, in 2024. This rich heritage is directly integrated into the sneaker’s aesthetic, featuring a dusty grey upper inspired by Lagos Island, breathable side panels crafted for the climate of Lagos, and a translucent pink outsole designed to evoke the city’s horizon at distinct moments of the day.

The release begins at the waf. flagship in Lagos and across all adidas retail and e-commerce platforms worldwide at $110. Launch time at the Lagos flagship: 9:00 a.m. WAT.

ABOUT WAF.

waf. (Wafflesncream) is Nigeria’s pioneering skate community and the first hub for skate culture in West Africa, combining a retail space with a creative community. For fourteen years, it has grown Lagos’ skate scene through community programming, retail, fashion, and music. In 2017, waf. launched Nigeria’s first Go Skate Day, now one of the country’s largest annual skate festivals.

ABOUT ADIDAS ORIGINALS

Inspired by the rich sporting heritage of adidas, one of the world’s leading sports brands and a global designer and developer of athletic footwear and apparel, adidas Originals is a lifestyle brand founded in 2001. With the adidas archive at its foundation, adidas Originals continues to evolve the brand’s legacy through its commitment to product innovation and its ability to filter the creativity and courage found on the courts and sporting arenas through the lens of contemporary youth culture.

item.content:encoded:
With four years remaining to the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals deadline, the Sustainability Table Discourse Series (STS) will mark its tenth anniversary on 15–16 October 2026 at the Balmoral Convention Centre, Federal Palace Hotel, Victoria Island, Lagos, with a deliberate shift from dialogue to delivery.

Under the theme ‘Leading the Sustainable Development Agenda: People, Planet and Prosperity,’ STS @10 will bring together leaders from government, business, finance, development institutions, technology and civil society to address a defining question: how can Africa bridge the gap between sustainable development ambition and execution?

Headlining the gathering is H.H. Muhammadu Sanusi II, Emir of Kano, who will deliver the Flagship Keynote, “People, Planet & Prosperity: The Decade of Delivery.”

The gathering will also feature H.E. Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat, Deputy Governor of Lagos State; Akintunde Oyebode, Commissioner for Finance, Ekiti State and Chairman, Forum of State Commissioners of Finance; H.E. Amb. Prof. (Mrs.) Olufolake AbdulRazaq, First Lady of Kwara State; Tenioye Majekodunmi, Director-General, National Council on Climate Change; Dr. Innocent Barikor, Director-General/CEO, NESREA; Rukaiya El-Rufai, Presidency / National Economic Council & Climate Change; Adam Boros, Vice President, Africa Finance Corporation; Ademola Ogunbanjo, President & CEO, Oando Clean Energy; Rolake Akinkugbe-Filani, CEO, EnergyInc Advisors Limited; and Dapo Otunla, Chief Corporate Services Officer, IHS Nigeria, among other leaders.

The current programme also features a high-level dialogue on mobilizing capital and leadership for Africa’s sustainability transition.

First convened in 2016, STS has spent a decade bringing together stakeholders around the green economy, climate finance, technology, circularity, food security, ESG and the Sustainable Development Goals. STS @10 marks an inflection point: a greater focus on bridging Africa’s sustainability implementation gap—the distance between commitments and action, innovation and scale, and viable projects and the investment required to deliver them.

“Africa does not suffer from a shortage of ambition, declarations or conferences. The real deficit is execution—turning policy into implementation, innovation into scale and credible projects into investible opportunities,” said Kayode Olaniyan, Convener of the Sustainability Table Discourse Series.

“Ten years of STS have shown us the power of bringing the right people to the table. But the next decade must be about what happens after they leave it. We are not convening another talk shop. The next decade must be aboutdelivery,” He added.

The programme will focus on four critical conversations: Nigeria’s energy future and expanding energy access; Technology, AI and the SDGs; the circular economy and responsible production; and resilient food systems, smarter value chains and cold-chain infrastructure.

Beyond the conversations, STS @10 will move from ideas to investment and innovation. Day Two will feature masterclasses, strategic investment engagements, the STS @10 Investment & Deals Room — Connecting Capital with Projects and Enterprise, and an Innovation Pitch Finale & Investor Showcase, creating opportunities to connect promising businesses and projects with financial institutions, investors and development partners.

The anniversary will also feature ‘The Earth Speaks’ Sustainability & Arts Exhibition, the launch of the commemorative coffee-table book A Decade at the Table: From Conversation to Transformation, and the premiere of the documentary Nigeria 2030: The Sustainability Imperative — A Decade of Dialogue. A New Era of Action.

The gala programme confirms both the book launch and documentary premiere as part of the anniversary celebrations.

Ten years ago, STS created a table for the conversation. At STS @10, the question is no longer simply who is at the table—but what gets done because they were there.

item.content:encoded:
On set for his Oba music video, Asake highlights his signature high-steeze look with a textured jacket and luxury travel accessories.

Music is a daily business in Nigeria, both for the artists making it and the listeners who keep up with new releases. Almost every week, new songs drop alongside music videos that bring them to life visually. This week, we’re putting you on five new music videos to check out, featuring Asake, Omah Lay, FOLA, and Young Jonn.

Here are five new Nigerian music videos that are worth adding to your watch list this week:

Asake – Oba

Asake takes fans into the creative process behind “Oba,” trading elaborate street scenes for a more intimate look at a late-night recording session. Directed by Director Buise, the video features the singer alongside producers and backing vocalists, while his signature style and confident presence reinforce the royal theme of the song. The track appears on his M$NEY album.

Omah Lay – Canada Breeze

Omah Lay’s “Canada Breeze” captures the singer’s reflective side, touching on personal growth, spirituality and finding peace after periods of worry. The song, from his Clarity of Mind album, pairs his signature melodic delivery with lyrics about moving beyond past struggles. Its music video gives fans another way to experience the record’s introspective mood.

FOLA – miss you ii

FOLA returns to matters of the heart with “miss you ii (nriri),” a release that speaks to longing and missing someone. The track features the Nigerian singer’s melodic Afropop style and arrives as part of a busy period for the rising artist, whose 9 album was released in October 2026. Fans can check out the song’s lyric video and follow its story through the lyrics.

Omah Lay – Artificial Happiness

Omah Lay takes a cinematic approach to “Artificial Happiness,” the opening track of his Clarity of Mind album. In the video, the singer awakens in an abandoned warehouse with a white tree at its centre, surrounded by mysterious figures whose movements give the scene an unsettling quality. Co-directed creatively by Omah Lay and his longtime collaborator NWSPK, the visual explores the song’s introspective world and the search for genuine happiness.

Young Jonn – Glass in the Air

Young Jonn brings dancefloor energy to “Glass in the Air.” The song reflects the excitement of navigating new territory and celebrating personal milestones, with the producer-turned-singer leaning into an upbeat, dance-ready sound. It is another opportunity to experience the infectious energy and melodic style that have become central to his evolution as an artist.

item.content:encoded:
Bimbo Ademoye and Timini Egbuson in western bridal styling for “My 30th Wedding”.

If it were rumoured that Bimbo Ademoye and Timini Egbuson are getting married, you’d hardly dismiss the rumour because of the times the duo have shared the stage in films, and their synergy and connection each time they appear together in a film. With their latest YouTube release, “My 30th Wedding” going viral, with over 22 million views in 11 days, it is informative to look at some of the films they have both featured in together.

In each film, you will find that connection. While they have mainly featured together in romance movies, the genre has not limited the creativity and energy they bring into each film. Let’s look at some of the films Bimbo Ademoye and Timini Egbuson have both featured in.

Breaded Life

In this 2021 movie, Bimbo Ademoye and Timini Egbuson navigate life in the ghetto after Timini’s character, Sunmi, is forced out of his wealthy existence. The film showcases the duo’s varying personas, highlighting themes of vulnerability, strength, and love. They demonstrate how two actors can continuously interact on screen while still delivering distinctly different vibes.

Reel Love

Produced by Timini Egbuson and directed by Kayode Kasum, Reel Love explores the relationship between love, celebrity and social media. Timini plays Tomide Jobi, a relationship influencer whose public image suffers after a heated confrontation with Rachel, played by T.J. Omusuku, goes viral. To repair the damage, Tomide agrees to stage a fake relationship with Rachel, but the arrangement becomes complicated when genuine feelings begin to develop. Bimbo Ademoye appears as Chizaram in the film, which also features Funke Akindele, Shaffy Bello and Dakore Egbuson-Akande. Released in Nigerian cinemas on Valentine’s Day in 2025, the film examines the pressure to maintain a public image and the difference between performing love for an audience and experiencing it in real life.

Big Love

In Big Love, Bimbo Ademoye and Timini Egbuson play Adina and Adil, two young people who meet while pursuing their ambitions and eventually fall in love. Adil is determined to achieve his dreams, while Adina is an independent woman focused on making a living. As their relationship develops, they must confront personal fears and a secret that threatens to come between them. Directed by Biodun Stephen, the romantic drama explores love, trust and the difficult choices that can test a relationship. The film also gives viewers another opportunity to see the chemistry between the two actors as romantic leads.

Unexpected Places

Bimbo Ademoye plays Prosper, the daughter of a housekeeper who steps in to manage the household while her mother recovers from surgery. Her new responsibilities bring her into contact with Chris, played by Timini Egbuson, a wealthy playboy whose irresponsible behaviour has become a concern for his father. Their relationship begins on difficult terms, but Prosper’s presence gradually challenges Chris to reconsider his choices and take responsibility for his life. Produced by Ademoye and directed by Great Val Edochie, the romantic drama explores personal growth, love and the unexpected circumstances that can change people’s lives. The film also takes a more emotional turn as the couple’s relationship develops.

Introducing the Kujus

Directed by Biodun Stephen, Introducing the Kujus is a family comedy-drama set in Badagry, Lagos. The film follows five siblings who are reluctant to return to their hometown for the fifth anniversary of their mother’s death. Mausi Kuju, played by Bisola Aiyeola, and her brother Maugbe, played by Timini Egbuson, devise a plan to bring the family together, but their complicated relationships threaten to get in the way. Bimbo Ademoye plays Ebi, one of the siblings whose relationships and family history contribute to the story. item.content:encoded:
Midea has announced the launch of WIN 9JA WIN, a nationwide consumer promotion designed to reward Nigerians who choose Midea home appliances during the 2026 festive shopping season. Running from 10 October to 31 December 2026, the promotion gives every qualifying shopper an instant opportunity to win, with a Chery Tiggo 2 Pro positioned as the ultimate grand prize.

Under the promotion, consumers who purchase any Midea product worth ₦100,000 or more from a participating dealer receive a scratch voucher at the point of purchase. The shopper scratches the voucher to reveal the reward won, creating a simple and immediate link between purchase and reward.

Every qualifying shopper is a winner, subject to the approved campaign terms and conditions. The campaign combines retail participation with radio, digital, public relations, in-store visibility and an extensive on-ground Promo Tour Truck programme.

The touring activation will carry the excitement of WIN 9JA WIN into selected markets and dealer locations, with the Chery Tiggo 2 Pro prominently showcased to give consumers a close view of the campaign’s headline prize.

A Consumer Promotion Built Around Instant Reward WIN 9JA WIN is designed to make the festive purchase journey more rewarding while strengthening engagement between Midea, its dealer network and consumers across Nigeria. Its central proposition is straightforward: make a qualifying purchase, receive a scratch voucher and discover the reward
immediately.

The approved reward pool spans Midea home appliances and branded consumer gifts. These include side-by-side refrigerators, chest freezers, air conditioners, refrigerators, washing machines, air fryers, microwave ovens, kettles, standing fans and blenders, as well as branded T-shirts, caps and pens. The ultimate reward is a Chery Tiggo 2 Pro, presented in the campaign materials as the car to be won.

MIDEA NIGERIA | MEDIA RELEASE 

How Consumers Can Participate 

Step 

Consumer action

Purchase

Buy any Midea product or combination of eligible Midea products  worth ₦100,000 or more from a participating dealer between 10  October and 31 December 2026.

Receive 

Collect the campaign scratch voucher issued for the qualifying  purchase.

Scratch 

Scratch the voucher to reveal the reward.

Claim

Follow the verification and prize-claim guidance provided by the  participating dealer in accordance with the approved campaign  terms and conditions.

Additional Midea Air Conditioner Offer

Alongside WIN 9JA WIN, Midea is also offering free installation and a free copper kit to consumers who purchase any Midea air conditioner from 1 October through 31 December 2026. The offer extends the campaign’s value beyond the product purchase by helping eligible AC buyers with installation support, subject to the applicable terms and conditions.

Promo Tour Truck Takes WIN 9JA WIN Closer to Consumers

A major feature of the campaign is the branded Promo Tour Truck programme, developed as a mobile visibility and engagement platform. The vehicle format is designed to operate as a moving billboard and activation hub, carrying Midea branding, product communication and WIN 9JA WIN messaging through high-traffic retail corridors and participating dealer locations.

The Chery Tiggo 2 Pro will be prominently showcased as part of the tour, allowing shoppers and local communities to see the campaign’s ultimate prize at close range. At scheduled dealer stops, consumers will be able to discover Midea products, receive clear information about the promotion and understand the qualifying purchase and scratch-voucher process. The programme is intended to support participating dealers, stimulate retail interest and bring the promotion into the communities where consumers shop.

Selected Tour Markets and Dealer Locations

The supplied tour schedule covers selected locations across Lagos, the South-West, South-South, South- East, North-Central and Northern Nigeria. The dealer activation routes are scheduled from 10 October to 1 November 2026, subject to final operational confirmation. The market clusters are listed below; the detailed dealer-location appendix forms part of this release pack.

East Route: Port Harcourt, Aba, Umuahia, Uyo and Oron, Owerri, Nnewi, Onitsha, Awka, Asaba and Enugu.

Lagos and adjoining markets: Lekki, Victoria Island, Ikoyi, Ajah, Lagos Island, Idumota, Apapa, Festac, Alaba, Ojo, Ikotun, Igando, Idimu, Ipaja, Abule Egba, Agege, Ikeja, Allen, Maryland, Ogba, Yaba, Surulere, Ebute Metta, Ikorodu, Badagry, Ota, Agbara and Isheri.

North and North-Central Route: Abuja, Mararaba, Lokoja, Makurdi, Lafia, Kaduna, Kano, Yola and Jimeta.

The campaign reflects Midea’s focus on making home-appliance technology more accessible and relevant to Nigerian households.

By combining guaranteed rewards with a wide dealer footprint and direct market engagement, WIN 9JA WIN gives consumers another reason to explore Midea’s range of air conditioners, refrigerators, freezers, washing machines, cooking appliances and small domestic appliances during the year-end season.

“WIN 9JA WIN is our way of thanking Nigerian consumers and making every qualifying purchase more rewarding. The mechanic is simple, transparent and immediate: buy, receive a scratch voucher and reveal your reward. Through the Promo Tour Truck programme, we are also taking the campaign closer to our dealer partners and consumers in markets across the country, while giving shoppers the opportunity to experience Midea products and see the Chery Tiggo 2 Pro grand prize up close.” – Ashok Dimri, Business Head, Africa, of Care Global Consumer Ltd.

Consumers can visit participating Midea dealers nationwide between 10 October and 31 December 2026, purchase eligible Midea products worth ₦100,000 or more and collect a scratch voucher to reveal their reward. Consumers purchasing any Midea air conditioner can also access the free installation and free copper kit offer through 31 December 2026, subject to the applicable terms and conditions.

Midea is one of over 10 brands operating under the Smart Home Business of Midea Group. Midea Group, with the vision of “bringing great innovations to life”, is an international tech-leading company which specializes in seven major business areas: Smart Home, Industrial Technologies, Building Technologies, KUKA, New Energy, Midea Healthcare and ANNTO Logistics. Midea’s products and services have served more than 500 million customers worldwide, including key clients and strategic partners across various industries. item.content:encoded:
TCL, a global leader in consumer electronics and No.1 Mini LED and Ultra Large Screen TV Brand (75”+)¹, has showcased its latest consumer electronics and home appliance portfolio for Nigeria during its West Africa regional launch event in Côte d’Ivoire.

Bringing together media, business partners, retailers, distributors, industry stakeholders and content creators from across the region, the event provided a closer look at TCL’s 2026 display innovations alongside new solutions across air conditioning, refrigeration, laundry and monitors.

The launch reflects TCL’s continued investment in Nigeria and its focus on introducing technologies that respond to the way consumers across both markets live today. From larger screens for sport and family entertainment to energy conscious cooling, high capacity appliances and connected home experiences, the new portfolio has been developed to combine performance, convenience and accessibility.

Daniel Ray, Director of Sales, TCL West Africa, said:

“Nigeria are important markets within TCL’s West Africa growth strategy, with consumers increasingly looking for technology that delivers strong performance while remaining relevant to their everyday needs. Our ambition is to continue making advanced technology more accessible while giving consumers greater choice across the home.“

Large screen entertainment continues to grow across Nigeria, with consumers increasingly seeking more immersive experiences across sport, movies, streaming and gaming.

For households conscious of both comfort and electricity consumption, the SaveIN AI Series offers a smarter approach to everyday cooling through intelligent controls and flexible energy management.

TCL’s latest refrigeration range addresses these priorities through generous capacity, flexible storage and reliable cooling, led by the P7 Side by Side Refrigerator and C7 Cross Door Refrigerator.

Its larger format makes it particularly suited to family households looking for greater storage flexibility without compromising on contemporary kitchen design.

The TCL C5 washer dryer combines a 12 kg washing capacity with TCL Super Drum technology, providing additional washing space and improved fabric movement. Its feature set includes Auto Dose, jetBubble technology, Wi Fi connectivity, Steam Wash, activeFresh, Dynamic Rinse and quick wash programmes.

The large capacity format is particularly suited to family households, while its connected features and automatic washing functions help reduce the effort required for everyday laundry and fabric care.

Strengthening TCL’s Presence Across Nigeria

The regional launch underlines TCL’s strategy to strengthen its presence across Nigeria through a broader product ecosystem and closer collaboration with local distributors, retailers, media and technology communities.

By combining global product innovation with a stronger understanding of local consumer priorities, TCL aims to deliver products that are relevant across different areas of everyday life, from entertainment and cooling to food storage, laundry and connected displays.

Daniel Ray added:

“Our focus is to strengthen TCL’s presence market by market, with products that respond to the needs of the consumers we serve. We see significant potential across both markets and will continue working closely with our partners to make TCL technology more widely available.”

item.title: “A Girl Who Learns Is a Girl Who Is Not a Bride” – Obiageli “Oby” Ezekwesili
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija Features
item.category: International Day of the Girl Child
item.description:
Obiageli “Oby” Ezekwesili for the International Day of the Girl Child.

The post “A Girl Who Learns Is a Girl Who Is Not a Bride” – Obiageli “Oby” Ezekwesili appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
A girl who learns is not a bride. Today, the world is asked to end child marriage and invest in girls’ rights. I join that call wearing three hats: as a member of the advisory council behind Columbia University’s report Accelerating Efforts to End Child Marriage; as Civil Society Representative on the Steering Committee of the African Union’s Decade of Accelerated Action for the Transformation of Education and Skills Development in Africa (2025–2034); and as the leader of Human Capital Africa, an organisation that has spent years arguing that Africa’s human capital crisis begins in the early-grade classroom.

UNICEF’s 2026 estimates show that about one in five girls worldwide is married before 18. That adds up to roughly 650 million women and girls alive today who were married as children. More than 12 million girls are still married each year, about one every three seconds, and sub-Saharan Africa has the highest prevalence at 31 per cent.

In Nigeria, 23.6 million women and girls were married before 18, the largest number in West and Central Africa. In parts of the North, the situation is a national emergency: in Jigawa, 78 per cent of women aged 20–49 were first married before 18, and 63 per cent of women left school to marry.

The cost of inaction is high. Our Columbia report includes new analysis by the Centre for Global Development. It estimates losses of up to $175 billion a year, or almost $2.5 trillion by 2040, from lost productivity and higher health risks caused by child marriage. The report also warns that aid cuts, weakening global commitment to women’s rights, and rising conflict could slow or reverse progress. Child marriage is not a side issue in development. It drains a nation’s human capital directly.

Progress is possible. An estimated 68 million child marriages have been averted over the past 25 years, through girls’ education, legal reform and social protection. The evidence on what works is strong:

  • Each year of secondary education lowers a girl’s chance of marrying before 18 by five percentage points or more.
  • In Niger, when the government removed the direct costs of middle school for rural girls, each additional year in secondary school was associated with a 19 percentage point lower probability of marriage.
  • If every African girl completed secondary education, child marriage could be almost eliminated.

Where HCA’s mission and this campaign meet, a girl cannot stay in secondary school if she never learned to read. Today, 89 per cent of children in sub-Saharan Africa are in learning poverty, unable to read and understand a simple text by age ten. A girl who cannot read by ten falls behind, then drops out. Once she is out of school, she is at the greatest risk of marriage. That is why we say schooling is not learning. Foundational literacy and numeracy are the first and cheapest protection a girl has.

At the Columbia launch, I said that community programmes and advocacy are not enough on their own. Governments must lead. On this Day of the Girl, Human Capital Africa calls on African governments to:

  • Make foundational learning a girl-protection policy. Every girl should be reading with comprehension by age ten, using proven methods such as structured pedagogy and Teaching at the Right Level.
  • Guarantee the move into secondary school. Remove fees, uniform and transport costs for girls, especially in rural communities with high rates of child marriage.
  • Enforce 18 as the minimum age of marriage in law and in practice, in every state and every community, with traditional and religious leaders as partners.
  • Fund this domestically. As foreign aid shrinks, African budgets and African philanthropy must take over.
  • Measure and publish. Track girls’ learning, their transition to secondary school, and child marriage rates in national accountability systems. The AU Decade of Education gives Africa ten years and a continental mandate. As a member of its Steering Committee, I will press for girls’ learning and retention to be at the centre of how the Decade’s success is measured. A Decade that does not end child marriage will not have transformed African education.

The Columbia report sets a realistic target: cutting child marriage prevalence from one in five to one in seven within five years. Africa can lead the way to that target, but only if we treat every girl’s classroom as the place where her childhood is protected.

Any girl-child should be a student, not a bride. She should learn, then lead.

The liquid dishwash and bar soap awards recognise its presence in two competitive household categories, while the Detergent Brand of the Decade award acknowledges the longer-term journey of its detergent business.

Speaking on the recognitions, Barbara Onianwah, Head of Marketing, Aspira Nigeria Limited, said the awards acknowledged the consistency required to build and sustain brands in a competitive market.

“These recognitions are meaningful because they reflect the consistency and work that go into building brands that remain relevant to consumers. The recognitions come as brands in Nigeria’s fast-moving consumer goods sector continue to respond to changing consumer preferences and increased competition across household-care categories.

item.content:encoded:
Ayra Starr performing at the NFL Halftime Show in London

There are not many great live performers in music. Some artists are very good but are only comfortable in the studio, which is understandable because music, like writing, is a solitary work and would require extra force or pull to stand before an audience and perform.

But there are also great live performers who, despite how good they are in the studio, are also comfortable bringing the music to a live audience. There is something special about that, watching an artist bring their music to life on stage. The vocals, the choreography, the stage presence, the connection with the audience — sometimes, a live performance makes you appreciate a song in an entirely new way.

There aren’t many with the artistry in Afrobeats. But Ayra Starr has made herself one of Afrobeats’ most exciting performers, and has constantly used the stage as another place to show the world her sability. From commanding festival stages and performing at major international music events to delivering memorable renditions of her biggest hits, Ayra Starr has continued to prove that her talent extends beyond the recording studio. She knows how to bring her music, personality, and energy together in a way that keeps audiences watching.

As her global profile continues to grow, with her recent 2026 NFL Halftime International Games performance in London, we’re looking back at some of Ayra Starr’s most iconic live performances:

item.content:encoded:
Ejovwoke Obas Olikuntuyi delivers a powerful performance as Ejiro in Her Daughters’ Mother

Nollywood is having an incredible global moment, and we couldn’t be prouder to cheer on our home-grown talents as they take their stories to the world. Filmmaker Chinazaekpere Chukwu is making her feature directorial debut with Her Daughters’ Mother, and the poignant Nigerian drama has been officially selected to screen at Film Africa 2026.

Scheduled for an October 28 screening at the newly launched EbonyLife Place London, the 110-minute feature explores womanhood, sacrifice, and the enduring bond between mothers and daughters.

Speaking on the emotional backbone of the project, Chinazaekpere Chukwu shared:

It’s intended to feel like a juxtaposition of ‘The Joys of Motherhood‘ by Buchi Emecheta and ‘Stay With Me’ by Ayọ̀bámi Adébáyọ̀. It reaches deep into the rights of women, how their lives are decided for them until the end, first by their families/spouses and finally by their kids.

Her Daughters’ Mother highlights the quiet resilience and domestic weight carried by women across generations.

Set against the rich cultural backdrop of Benin and filmed early this year in English, Pidgin, Urhobo, and Bini, the story follows 33-year-old Ejiro (played by Ejovwoke Obas Olikuntuyi). After being married off at the tender age of 16, Ejiro returns home in her thirties as a widowed mother of two daughters, determined to secure a brighter future for them.

Faced with limited options, she enters a second marriage with Osato (Philip Asaya), a lorry driver who promises security and education for her girls in exchange for a male heir. However, when Ejiro struggles to fulfill his demands, Osato’s entitlement turns her life into a nightmare, leaving her longing for the freedom she last felt as a child. Meanwhile, her eldest daughter Ejaita (Osas Okonyon), a bright 16-year-old dreaming of becoming a doctor, struggles against her mother’s overprotectiveness, unaware of the immense sacrifices being made on her behalf.

Osas Okonyon stars as Ejaita, a bright teenager whose ambitious dreams clash with her mother’s protective sacrifices.

The film boasts an exceptional cast, including Najite Dede and Adeoluwa Akintoba. Behind the scenes, Chukwu—who wrote the screenplay alongside Sunday Melvin Iwinosa from a story by Efosa Ogbomo—collaborated with cinematographer Yinka Adegoke, executive producer and co-producer Efosa Ogbomo, and story consultant and editor Joshua Tsotso.

Adeoluwa Akintoba in a scene from Her Daughters’ Mother, exploring youth and ambition.

Chukwu’s transition to feature filmmaking follows her award-winning streak at the EbonyLife Creative Academy, where she graduated with the Best Director award for A Psalm for Abigail, as well as her standout short film Ti e Nbo, which screened in the Shorts category at AFRIFF in 2023. Produced by One Child Grace Studio in association with C.A.N.O Productions, Uncut Gem Productions, and Nka Pictures, Her Daughters’ Mother promises to deliver a deeply moving, authentic Nigerian narrative that resonates across borders.

item.content:encoded:
The Leo Stan Ekeh Foundation (LSEF) has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Nigeria Computer Society (NCS) to provide mentorship, technical training and real-world technology experience to the Nigerian whiz kids under the Foundation’s technology scholarship initiative.

The 1000 scholarship scheme, which was first announced by Africa’s foremost technology entrepreneur and Chairman of Zinox Group, Leo Stan Ekeh, is designed to empower indigent but exceptionally gifted Nigerian students to study Computer Science and other technology-related disciplines in federal and state universities, as well as polytechnics, across the country.

The scholarship reflects Dr. Ekeh’s philosophy of “one family, one tech-empowered person” and will support 1,000 students selected from all 36 states of the federation and the Federal Capital Territory, irrespective of ethnic background.

From their first year through graduation, beneficiaries will receive world-class technology training, skills development and monthly financial support. Each scholar will also have a dedicated mentor to provide guidance throughout their academic journey.

Under the MoU, the NCS will provide technical support and practical learning through experienced and certified technology professionals. The programme will blend academic learning with real-world exposure, helping beneficiaries build technical competence, problem-solving skills and the confidence to apply their knowledge beyond the classroom.

According to the Director of LSEF, Dr. George Emetuche, the programme will feature boot camps each semester, creating opportunities for students to learn beyond the classroom and gain practical experience. The objective, he explained, is to prepare beneficiaries not merely to graduate, but to become capable technology professionals who can solve real-world problems.

Speaking at the ceremony, NCS President, Professor Muhammed Siraju Aliyu, described Dr. Leo Stan Ekeh as a nationalist who has consistently supported initiatives that create opportunities for Nigerians who may otherwise lack access.

He noted that Dr. Ekeh’s relationship with the NCS predates the scholarship initiative and has contributed to the advancement of technology and human capital development. He also highlighted Dr. Ekeh’s technology innovation programmes, which identify young people with ideas, support them in developing their concepts and create opportunities for them to pitch to potential investors.

Professor Aliyu expressed appreciation for Dr. Ekeh’s contributions to the NCS and reaffirmed the Society’s commitment to initiatives that support national growth and development.

Representing the Zinox Group, Executive Director, Human Resources, Mrs. Chioma Nwoke, assured the Foundation and the NCS of the Group’s continued support for the initiative, cohort after cohort.

Beyond the scholarship, the programme represents a long-term investment in Nigeria’s human capital. By helping 1,000 gifted young Nigerians gain access to quality education, technology skills, mentorship and practical experience, the initiative can contribute to a stronger pipeline of home-grown technology professionals, innovators and problem-solvers.

item.content:encoded:

Permission to call Nancy Isime Madam EP? Because the Nollywood star has just announced that she is stepping into a new role, and this time, she will be calling some of the shots behind the camera. Nancy is making her debut as an executive producer, taking on a new side of filmmaking after years of entertaining us on screen.

You know her from films and series such as Blood Sisters, Shanty Town, Kambili: The Whole 30 Yards, Superstar and Obama‘M. Now, Nancy wants us to follow her as she takes on the business of making a film, from the early meetings to sponsorship discussions and marketing. And she is letting us in on the process from the very beginning.

In the video announcing the news, Nancy wore a brown outfit with an oversized collar, structured shoulders and gathered balloon sleeves. She paired it with a gold leaf statement necklace and finger-wave hair, looking ready for the boardroom before getting into the business of filmmaking. But beyond the outfit, it was what she had to say that got us listening.

Nancy Isime marks her transition behind the camera as an executive producer in a custom metallic brown dress with a flounced hem.

“Well yes, you’ve known me as an actor. But this time, I’m stepping into a completely new chapter. This is my first production as executive producer!”

And while she is excited about the new role, Nancy is not pretending she has everything figured out. She admitted that taking this step comes with a few nerves, saying, “Oh my God, guys, I can’t lie… I’ve never… my heart is doing gbi-gbi-gbi-gbi-gbi. Can I do this? Can I do this? Am I ready? Shall we?”

The announcement also comes with glimpses of Nancy stepping out for corporate engagements, attending meetings, getting styled on set and speaking with camera operators. It looks like we will be seeing a lot more of what happens on the production side, rather than only the finished work on screen.

And since she has invited us behind the scenes, we are curious to see how this first production comes together. Madam EP, we are following!

Kimberly Jael posing in a black, yellow, and red evening gown for Uganda Independence Day.

Black sequins, sunshine yellow and a long red train? Kimberly Jael has found a gorgeous way to wear Uganda’s national colours. The model and Miss Universe Uganda 2026 first runner-up marked the country’s 64th Independence Day on 9 October in a sculpted gown that takes inspiration from the Ugandan flag.

Let’s start with that corset. The strapless black bodice is covered in sequins, with lace trimming the neckline, while canary-yellow fabric falls across her chest and shoulders. Then, at the hips, crimson-red fabric gathers before flowing into a fitted mermaid skirt that trails along the floor. Each colour has its place, and the long red train gives the look an extra flourish.

Tiny pearl embellishments add detail to the face art, while her cropped natural afro leaves room for her large drop earrings, finished with traditional cowrie shells.

But Kimberly’s choices go beyond matching her outfit to the flag. She explained the meaning behind the gown in a message celebrating Uganda’s independence, connecting its details to the country’s history, the sacrifices of previous generations and the hopes she has for its future.

Independence is not just a date, it’s the chains that were broken and blood that was shed!!!

The glam is intentional. The pearls are for every tear my ancestors shed. The sequins are for every star in our future. The red train is long because our journey was long. This is what 64 years of resilience looks like in high fashion.

Happy Independence Day Uganda — we are not just free, we are FASHIONABLY FREE!

How do you balance it?

That is one of the first questions women ask when they meet another woman who seems to have it all: the career, the family, the side projects, the composure. I understand the question. I’ve asked it myself. But the longer I live, the more convinced I am that we are asking for something that does not exist.

When we ask for balance, we are really asking for the two sides of the scale to weigh the same, all the time. Equal weight to work and home. Equal weight to ambition and rest. Equal weight to the people who need the self and us we are trying not to lose. A scale, perfectly level, held steady every single day.

But nothing honest works that way.

Consider this: every major system of thought humanity has ever built carries a trade-off; a cost baked into its benefit. Prioritise individual freedom, and you risk the collective; protect the collective, and you constrain the individual. There has never been a framework, political or economic or moral, that delivered every good thing at once with no side effect. That is why no government pleases all its people, and why even the most admired ideas have always had their critics. If perfect balance cannot be engineered into our grandest theories, why do we expect to achieve it in a single human life, lived in real time, with finite hours?

Balance, I’ve come to believe, is a myth. Not a lie exactly, but a mirage. You cannot give one hundred per cent to everything simultaneously. Something always gives. The only real question is whether you are choosing what gives, or letting it be chosen for you.

So I’ve stopped chasing balance. I’ve started practising seasons.

In every season of life, the demands are weighted differently. There are seasons when work must take more. Seasons when family must. Seasons of building, and seasons of recovering. The wisdom is not in holding all things equal; it is in reading accurately which season you are in, and letting your energy follow it without guilt.

Within each season, there is a second discipline, one borrowed from an analogy many will know: learning to tell your glass balls from your rubber ones. Some of the things we juggle are rubber. If you drop them, they bounce. The deadline that can shift. The event you can miss. The email that can wait till Monday. They feel urgent, but they recover.

Others are glass. Drop them, and they crack, sometimes beyond repair. Your health. A child’s childhood. A marriage. Your integrity. Certain relationships and certain moments that do not come round again. The tragedy is how often we exhaust ourselves protecting the rubber balls, answering every message, meeting every expectation, saying yes to everything, while a glass ball slips from the other hand.

Knowing the difference is the real skill. Not balance. Triage. So when someone asks me how I balance it all, my honest answer is: I don’t. Nobody does. What I try to do instead is stay awake to my season, and clear-eyed about which balls in my hands are glass.

Some days I get it right. Some days a glass ball wobbles and I catch it just in time. Some days I let a rubber one fall on purpose, and feel the strange relief of choosing. That, I think, is the most any of us can do. Not a perfectly level scale, but a steady pair of hands, and the wisdom to know what must never be allowed to break.

item.content:encoded:
Nigerian poet and lawyer Ogaga Ifowodo has won the 2026 Nigeria Prize for Literature, sponsored by Nigeria LNG Limited (NLNG), for his poetry collection, Why Does God Need a Gun?

Ifowodo’s win adds to a distinguished literary career spanning several decades. His other poetry collections include Homeland and Other Poems, which won the 1993 Association of Nigerian Authors (ANA) Poetry Prize; Madiba, which won the 2003 ANA/Cadbury Poetry Prize; The Oil Lamp, which won the 2005 ANA/Gabriel Okara Poetry Prize; and A Good Mourning, which was shortlisted for the Nigeria Prize for Literature in 2017.

The 2026 edition of the Nigeria Prize for Literature focused on poetry and attracted 223 submissions. Ifowodo’s winning collection emerged from a final shortlist that included James Ngwu Eze’s Unbind Me Now and Tares Oburumu’s Flora’s Love Colony.

NLNG’s Nigerian Prize for Literature is the biggest literary award on the continent, and the award comes with a $100,000 cash prize.

Nigerian singer FOLA has expressed his appreciation for renowned author Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie and music legend 2Baba for their contributions to his sophomore album, 9.

On the album’s second track, how many, FOLA samples a portion of Adichie’s Harvard speech, in which she reflects on the relationship between fear, self-doubt, and creativity. “Procrastinating is a form of fear, and it is difficult to acknowledge fear. But the truth is that you cannot create anything of value without both self-doubt and self-belief,” she says in the excerpt.

The singer also samples 2Baba’s popular song, If Love Is A Crime, on crime, the 11th track on FOLA’s second album, paying homage to one of Nigeria’s most influential musicians and his enduring contribution to the country’s music scene.

Taking to X (formerly Twitter), FOLA shared his gratitude to both figures, writing, “Today, I’m beyond grateful to Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie and the legendary 2Baba for their contribution to the arts, their blessings on my sophomore, and for leaving my generation multiple standards to aspire to.”

item.content:encoded:
Sometimes, when two artists find themselves together in a studio, they find it difficult to spark a connection. They can make a song together, but it might feel like climbing a cliff if they try to make another song. Meanwhile, some artists have that connection, that synergy, that whenever they find each other in the studio, they produce magic. They make beautiful, sweet music. For instance, Wizkid and Asake, who have not only featured one another on each other’s albums, Morayo and Lungu Boy, respectively, but have also released a joint project, an EP. As Wizkid puts it in their interview, they have had “successful collaborations.” There are artists like that who find creativity in the other’s creativity.

So are BNXN and FOLA, whose music, when carefully compared in terms of lyricism, could be considered the same. They do not sound the same; no, two artists can never sound the same, but you could always imagine BNXN on a FOLA, and vice versa. And they have shown their fans that whenever they find each other on a song, there is always a synergy. Actually, FOLA sang in “how many“, off his sophomore album, ‘9‘, “Mo Korin bi BNXN,” which means, I sing like BNXN.

The journey began with the remix of FOLA’s hit song, Alone, and BNXN was featured. The collaboration introduced listeners to what would become one of the more interesting musical partnerships in Nigerian Afrobeats. BNXN brought his familiar, soulful delivery to the song, complementing FOLA’s smooth vocals and emotional approach to music.

Then came Very Soon, a song on BNXN’s 2025 album, Captain, which featured FOLA. This time, FOLA joined BNXN on his own record, returning the favour and showing that their connection was not limited to one artist’s sound. They could find each other on either side of a collaboration and still make it work. Their musical relationship continued with Shamaya, another joint recording on BNXN’s Still in Charge EP.

Now, the two artists have reunited on my type, a song on FOLA’s sophomore album, 9, released on October 9, 2026. But for listeners who have followed BNXN and FOLA’s journey together, “My Type” is another opportunity to enjoy a pairing that has consistently found room for both artists to shine.

BNXN and FOLA have given their listeners reasons to always look forward to what they might create together next. If their collaborations so far are anything to go by, this is one musical partnership worth keeping an eye on. For now, fans will enjoy BNXN’s latest EP, Still in Charge and FOLA’s sophomore album: the 14-track project that features other notable Nigerian and African artists, including Davido, Ayra Starr, Darkoo, Bella Shmurda and Zlatan.

Ten years ago, Power Oil invited Nigerians to take a step for their hearts in celebration of World Heart Day. A decade later, that step has become a movement. The 10th edition of WalkHeartOn, held on October 1, 2026, at The Stables Sports Ground, Surulere, Lagos, brought together thousands of people for a day centred on fitness, heart health, community and fun.

The milestone edition recorded 25,536 registrations, with 11,896 people physically attending. From early-morning fitness activities and health checks to music, games, refreshments and entertainment, WalkHeartOn 10.0 created an experience that showed that prioritising your health does not have to be boring. 

Commenting on the milestone, Roland Akpe, Marketing Manager, Oils and Fats Portfolio at Tolaram, said,

“For 10 years, WalkHeartOn has been a reflection of Power Oil’s commitment to helping Nigerians live healthier lives, reminding us that caring for our hearts goes beyond what we eat. It is also about staying active, moving more and making healthier choices every day. As we celebrate World Heart Day and a decade of WalkHeartOn, we are proud to have created a platform that brings Nigerians together to take meaningful steps towards healthier hearts.”

For many attendees, it was a chance to exercise with friends and family. For others, it was an opportunity to meet new people, enjoy performances and simply step away from the usual routine. But beneath all the excitement was the message that has driven WalkHeartOn for a decade: every step towards a healthier lifestyle matters. Over the years, the annual walk has evolved from a fitness event into a community-driven platform that encourages Nigerians to make heart health part of their everyday lives.

item.title: Women Innovators Building Smarter Ways to Live, Eat and Stay Healthy in Africa
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
By Bayer Foundation and Impact Hub

The post Women Innovators Building Smarter Ways to Live, Eat and Stay Healthy in Africa appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Across Africa, some of the most interesting solutions to everyday problems are being built by women who have experienced those problems up close.

A doctor sees patients struggling to access cardiac screening and builds an AI-powered ECG device. A nurse watches patients lose hours navigating the healthcare system and creates a digital platform to make it easier. A food entrepreneur sees farmers lose the value of their harvest and builds the processing infrastructure they need.

An agronomist looks at Morocco’s water crisis and asks a different question: what if we could grow more food with far less water? These are the stories behind five of the 15 women named as 2026 Bayer Foundation Women Entrepreneurs Award winners globally, powered by the Impact Hub Network.

The five African awardees come from Kenya, Ethiopia, Nigeria and Morocco, joining 10 other women entrepreneurs selected from across Latin America and Asia.

From Kenya and Ethiopia to Nigeria and Morocco, their businesses are rethinking how communities access healthcare, preserve food and adapt to a changing climate. Each will receive €25,000 in non-dilutive funding alongside a six-month accelerator designed to help them strengthen their businesses and take their solutions further.

Meet the women behind the ideas

Dr. Alice Muhuhu of Aurora Health Systems, Kenya

Alice started Aurora Health Systems after seeing patients arrive at the hospital with advanced heart conditions that could have been detected much earlier.

Her answer is an AI-powered, portable ECG device designed to work offline and in low-resource clinics. It can detect more than 50 cardiac conditions and is already being used across more than 100 clinics in Kenya. But Alice is also tackling another problem in healthcare: whose data gets represented. Less than 1% of global ECG data comes from African populations, so Aurora is building a large-scale African cardiology dataset to help develop technology that better reflects the people it is intended to serve.

Beamlak Alemayehu of Medanit Digital Health, Ethiopia

For Beamlak, the healthcare problem was not always whether treatment existed. Sometimes, it was simply finding it. The former clinical nurse and social worker founded Medanit after seeing patients travel long distances, wait hours, and move between hospitals and pharmacies just to find the right care.

Medanit brings those services together through an app, website, and low-bandwidth call centre, allowing people to connect with doctors, medication, and mental health services without requiring everyone to have the same level of internet access or digital literacy.

In 2025, the platform reached more than 58,000 users and onboarded over 500 doctors and 60 healthcare partners.

Funmilayo Ishola  of Dehydrator Hub, Nigeria

Funmilayo grew up watching her mother trade fresh produce in Lagos markets and saw how quickly food could lose its value when there was nowhere to process or preserve it. That experience inspired Dehydrator Hub, which gives small food businesses and farmers access to solar-powered dehydrators, packaging equipment and technical training without requiring them to buy the machinery themselves.

More than 75 tonnes of fruit and vegetables have already been processed through the model, while farmers using the service have recorded income increases of 30–35%. Funmilayo has also trained more than 3,000 women.

Her bigger vision is to establish 776 processing hubs across Nigeria, one for every local government area.

Sokayna Bellam of Jodoor Greentech, Morocco

For Sokayna, the future of food begins with a simple question: how do you keep farming when water is becoming harder to find? The agronomist founded Jodoor Greentech to explore that question through hydroponic farming. The company now operates 10 greenhouses across 3,500 square metres, producing around 100 tonnes of fresh produce annually.

The system uses up to 90% less water than conventional farming and eliminates chemical pesticides. For Morocco and other water-stressed regions, it offers a glimpse of what agriculture could look like when farmers have to produce more with considerably less.

Omowunmi Emmanuel-Ogah of ExCare Health, Nigeria

During the COVID-19 pandemic, pharmacist Omowunmi encountered a mother who rushed into her pharmacy with her sick four-year-old son because she had nowhere else to turn.

The experience made her think differently about what a community pharmacy could be. Today, ExCare Health combines pharmacy services with diagnostics, vaccination and primary care. It operates five pharmacies, two diagnostic laboratories and an accredited immunisation centre across Lagos and Ogun State. Through its Vaxreach programme, ExCare has also helped turn eight pharmacies across five states into vaccination hubs.

Omowunmi’s ambition is to show what could happen if Nigeria’s thousands of community pharmacies became part of the country’s primary healthcare infrastructure. Supporting women to take good ideas further.

What connects these five women is not simply that they are working in technology, healthcare, or agriculture. It is that their businesses started with problems they could see around them.

The Bayer Foundation Women Entrepreneurs Award is designed to help founders like these move from solving a local problem to reaching more people. Since 2021, the Bayer Foundation has supported women-led enterprises in health and food security through non-dilutive funding, networks and structured support for growth.

Through its partnership with the Impact Hub Network, the programme adds local entrepreneurial networks, mentorship and access to a wider community of impact-driven founders.

For the 2026 awardees, the next chapter is about scale: taking solutions that are already working and figuring out how far they can go.

item.content:encoded:
As BellaNaija turned 20 this year, we reinforced one important thing: strengthening the core the platform started with. BN was launched to showcase Africa’s beauty to the world through stories, fashion and weddings. To deepen this commitment, everything we have done this year reinforces the platform’s foundations. From the recent Grand Red Carpet Experience, tagged High Fashion Icon, which is an avenue to celebrate Africa’s vibrant culture, to On Our Radar, a series I launched in August to spotlight a few Nigerian artists whose distinct voices are projected to define Afrobeats in the future.

Through August and September, four artists were spotlighted, each sharing what inspired them to start making music and their absolute dream with music. The series was launched to further strengthen what BellaNaija is known for, which is showcasing African creatives to the world, even before they become global.

The spotlights are as follows:

Solana

For Solana, music has always been a natural way to express herself. She began writing songs at six and took her first steps towards making music professionally while at university, after her roommate introduced her to a recording studio. She describes her sound as YoruPop, an experimental blend that allows her to explore different sounds, emotions, and ideas without being confined to one genre. Her ultimate dream is to share African culture with the world through music that remains authentic to her roots, inspires people to embrace who they are, and leaves a lasting cultural impact.

Read her feature here.

Firstklaz

Firstklaz grew up surrounded by music, but it was seeing people connect with his songs, sing his lyrics back to him, and relate to his stories that convinced him to pursue it as a career. His sound blends African rhythms and Hausa culture with modern Afrobeats production, bringing together traditional melodies, storytelling, and contemporary influences. Beyond chart success and awards, his dream is to reach a global audience, sell out concerts around the world, create music that people will return to for decades, and inspire a new generation of African artists to embrace their cultural identities.

Read his feature here.

Abefe

Music has been a part of Abefe’s life since childhood, and his passion for singing eventually found a wider audience through his TikTok covers and relatable, vulnerable storytelling. His songs offer listeners a glimpse into his thoughts, experiences, and perspectives on life, allowing them to connect with the person behind the music. For Abefe, success means being able to shut down London’s O2 Arena with ease — a bold ambition that reflects his desire to grow from an emerging artist into a major name on the global music scene.

Read his feature here.

KW33N B

KW33N B, also known as B3NEDICTA, grew up surrounded by music, but discovering that she could create her own songs from her thoughts, emotions, and experiences made her see music as more than a passion. It became an outlet for self-expression and a place where she felt understood. Her sound blends Afrobeats, soul, and pop, drawing inspiration from everyday life and the human experience. Her ultimate dream is to share her music with the world, connect with people across cultures, and create timeless songs that bring listeners happiness, comfort, and a sense of connection long after their release.

Read her feature here.

item.content:encoded:
A young man rests on a stack of books at a desk, sunlight filtering through a window. Photo Credit: Oladimeji Ajegbile/Pexels.

They buried Ebiakpo’s father, Papa, in June. The rain that day was the small, annoying kind that did not commit. Papa had taught History for thirty-one years. When he died, the state owed him nineteen months of salary and a pension nobody could prove existed. Ebiakpo was the third of four children, and the scholar. That was his role. His father’s small revenge on a country that had refused to pay him: he would build one more of himself, and this one would be paid what he was owed. Ebiakpo read Law. First class.

In August, he went for an interview at a firm on Victoria Island. The partner who saw him spent twenty minutes bragging about representing a luxury influencer accused of beating two girlfriends and turning up at his own arraignment high. The firm offered Ebiakpo 130,000 naira a month. Transport alone would have eaten seventy. On the bus home, he did the arithmetic and understood, for the first time, that his father had not died of a stroke.

His eldest brother Tamunotonye did the thing they did not name. He now called himself Chief Dollar Papi Money and had it airbrushed onto the boot of the BMW X6 he parked sideways at family functions. His large diamond chain hung to his navel. His girlfriend, Blessed, came with him everywhere, in a waist-length lace-front, acrylics she could barely type with, and a BBL he paid doctors in Turkey to install, as rumours had it. The chain around her neck hung a huge pendant that spelt Quila B — half for tequila, which was the only thing she drank, and half for the American popstar she was studying to become.

Chief Dollar took Ebiakpo to a place on the island where the drinks cost more than Ebiakpo’s rent. “Bro”, he said, wiping his mouth, “survival for this country no be grammar again. Na money. Na feeding your people. School na the biggest client Nigeria don ever run”. At the next table, a boy was livestreaming and shouting at his own phone. When the waitress bent to ask him softly to lower his voice, he turned and told her, at full volume, that a girl her size should be grateful he was patronising the restaurant she cleaned. His table applauded.

The second brother, Preye, had broken Papa’s heart. He read Engineering at the University of Portharcout but left in his third year to do music. He did not do music. He managed a boy from the streets called Flexable, who could not finish a sentence in any language. Flexable’s last single had crossed five million streams in a week. Preye carried Flexable’s water bottle and towels to shows and said he was investing in the brand. Papa never once asked him about the music.

Before he died, Papa said one afternoon in the parlour, while watching TV. “This country no longer celebrates excellence. It now rewards performed foolishness, because foolishness travels faster on the internet than sense.”

Ebiakpo’s sister, Papa’s only daughter, Tarilaye, was fifteen. She did not know the capital of Taraba. When he told her Jalingo, she said no; she was sure Jalingo was a dance, then thought about it and said sorry, that one was Alingo, and laughed at herself for a whole minute. Her plan, she had told their mother, was to become an influencer first, then a reality-show girl, then to marry a musician, or possibly an actor; she was still deciding.

Tarilaye had been the brilliant one. Before Papa died, she had read all Chinua Achebe cover to cover at eleven and even corrected her teachers in school. But school na scam had become a hymn in her generation, and she quietly stopped trying. She turned instead to endless scrolling and devotion to the lives of celebrities who did not know her name. She was happier now, or something that looked from a distance like happier.

The Yoruba word for one who knows zero used to be the worst thing a boy could call another in a schoolyard — Olodo. Now the ones who know zero owned everything the market would price. Ebiakpo’s first-class certificate lived in a drawer. It smelled faintly of batteries. One night, Ebiakpo had dreamt his father was still teaching. The classroom was empty. He was writing on the board in his beautiful handwriting, and behind him, through the window, the whole country was dancing.

He woke, and started thinking about which of his father’s children was the actual dullard.
